transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Halcyon AI), Jon Ruiz (Halcyon infra), Ellen Park (Halcyon CTO)

Summary: quick discovery focused on model selection for Halcyon's multi-lingual assistant product. Main topics: open model comparisons (Llama3 vs Mistral vs Falcon), context length needs (8k vs 32k vs 128k), multilingual quality (EN, ES, FR, JA), and tool-calling / function call support. Discussed deployment options (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private) with security and routing concerns.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:07] Maya: Hey Alex, doing well. Thanks. We have about 45 minutes, want to walk through our stack and constraints.
[00:12] Priya: Great. Quick agenda: learn about your use case, talk model selection and context length, then deployment options and next steps. Is that good?
[00:20] Ellen: Yep sounds good. I'll jump in on infra questions.
[00:24] Jon: Same — I'll focus on networking, peering, and benchmarks.

[00:30] Alex: Maya, can you give a brief on the product?
[00:33] Maya: Sure. We're building a conversational assistant for customer support across 6 languages right now — EN, ES, FR, PT, JA and KR. Latency targets: sub-400ms median for turn-by-turn with 1.5–2k token responses on average. We also need the model to do structured tool calls — ticket creation, internal DB lookups, and call some external APIs. Privacy is important — some customers require data residency, and we'll need SOC2 level controls.

[01:05] Priya: Great, that's helpful. For model selection, are you leaning open models or more managed closed models?
[01:11] Maya: We prefer open models for cost and control. Our main options internally are Llama3 variants, Mistral 7B/Chat, and Falcon 40B. We also consider Redwood's hosted catalog — but we need to validate multilingual quality.

[01:25] Priya: Ok. A few things we typically discuss: 1) effective context length and whether you need long context (32k/64k/128k), 2) tokenization differences for Asian languages, 3) tool-calling support — do you need standard HTTP webhook style or structured function-calls with schemas?

[01:40] Maya: We need function-style calls with strict schema validation for downstream automation. Also we have long context for conversation + 3–4 doc lookups per session, so we might need 64k in some flows.

[01:53] Alex: On Redwood's side, hosted supports a catalog of open models and we can route requests to Dedicated pools or Private installs. For long-context workloads we have kernel selection and KV cache optimization to keep latency predictable. But we should benchmark with your prompt sets.

[02:10] Jon: On networking/security, if we go Private we need to know about KMS/HSM integration and audit logs. Are those available?

[02:18] Priya: Yes — Private includes KMS integration (customer-managed keys), full audit logs, and SSO/SAML. Our SOC 2 docs cover data at rest and transit. For Dedicated, we provide VPC peering and tiled IP ranges — we can share network design.

[02:33] Ellen: For Hosted, what's your data retention policy? We can't ingest PII for some customers.

[02:38] Alex: Hosted can be configured with short retention and opt-out for data usage. For stricter requirements we'd recommend Dedicated or Private with contractual commitments. We'll toss SOC2 and retention docs in the follow-up.

[02:48] Maya: Back to models — can you summarize where Llama3 vs Mistral vs Falcon typically win?

[02:52] Priya: Sure. Roughly speaking: Llama3 chat variants often have strong instruction-following and are good cross-lingual, but larger parameter models increase cost. Mistral is very good for short responses and is cost-effective; new versions have improved multilingual support. Falcon 40B tends to be strong for generation quality and context, but is heavier and costs more in Dedicated. Tokenization varies — some models handle Japanese/Korean differently making effective token counts higher.

[03:21] Maya: Our language mix is approx 55% EN, 20% ES, 10% FR, 10% PT, 3% JA, 2% KR. Response length average 1.5k tokens, but some cases hit 5–10k when we include docs.

[03:35] Priya: That distribution helps. For the 5–10k cases we recommend either a 64k context model or using Redwood's prefix/KV cache so you can store doc embeddings and only send deltas. For tool-calls, we support function calling semantics similar to OpenAI's function calling; we can map to your schema and validate before downstream actions.

[03:58] Jon: How does Redwood handle fallbacks when Dedicated capacity is full? We need SLA guarantees and graceful degradation.

[04:04] Alex: We offer routing policies — you can prefer Dedicated but fail over to hosted or lower-capacity model variants. For SLA we have Dedicated commitments in reserved capacity contracts. We'll go over exact P99 latency SLOs in the follow-up.

[04:18] Maya: Benchmarking is key. We want to run a candidate set: Llama3-Chat-32k, Mistral-Chat-7B, Falcon-40B, and a quantized 40B variant to see cost/latency tradeoffs. Does Redwood run benchmarks in our VPC or do you need test traffic to your hosted infra?

[04:33] Priya: We can do both. For Hosted/Dedicated we can run synthetic and replayed prompt sets from our side against your representative workload. For Private, we can provide a benchmark package you run in your environment or we can run with a temporary peered test environment. We'll need representative prompt files and a sample user distribution.

[04:53] Jon: We'll need a security-friendly option — probably peered testing with allowed IPs.

[04:57] Ellen: Another question: how do you manage quantization and accuracy regressions? We can't have a silent drop in intent recognition after switching to an int8 profile.

[05:05] Priya: Great point. Redwood Optimize suggests quantization profiles per workload. We run quality checks against prompt sets and have regression alerts — you can pin to a known good profile and roll out canaries. We also provide eval hooks to run unit tests whenever you change quantization or model variants.

[05:23] Maya: Any limitations on function calls for long context models? We need real-time schema validation and ability to reference earlier turns.

[05:29] Priya: Function calls are supported across our catalog. For long context we keep KV cache references to earlier turns so the model can reference conversation history without resending full context. There are some kernel-specific constraints for very large contexts that affect latency; that's why benchmarking with your prompts is important.

[05:46] Alex: For pricing, typical hosted unit economics differ from Dedicated — hosted is metered per token/embedding; Dedicated is monthly reserved GPUs plus usage. We'll send a tailored pricing comparison.

[05:58] Maya: Do you support multilingual embeddings for retrieval? Our retrieval pipeline uses embeddings and vector DB. We currently use an off-the-shelf multilingual embedder.

[06:06] Priya: We support multilingual embeddings in the catalog and can recommend pairings. We often pair a cost-effective multilingual embedder with a higher-capacity generative model, or use the same model family for both depending on quality needs. We also integrate with common vector DBs.

[06:19] Jon: About monitoring — what observability do you expose for per-request latency / token cost? We need per-route dashboards, traces, and message-level cost breakdown.

[06:28] Alex: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, per-model latency distributions, traces, and per-route dashboards. You can set alerts for quality regressions tied to prompt-set evals.

[06:36] Maya: A smaller nit — we saw references to "Redwood Dedicate" in past docs. Is product name Dedicated or Dedicate?

[06:41] Alex: Sorry about that, some older slides say "Redwood Dedicate" — correct name is Redwood Dedicated. Apologies for the typo in older materials.

[06:48] Maya: No worries, just wanted to clarify.

[06:51] Priya: Next for us: to run a meaningful benchmark we need your prompt set, language distribution, and expected concurrency. Also helpful: tokenization differences per language (we can produce token estimates after we run tokenizer sampling).

[07:03] Maya: Concurrency is bursty — baseline 60 RPS, peaks to 400 RPS during campaigns. Latency SLOs are per-turn <400ms median; P95 is less critical but we want to avoid >1.5s often.

[07:16] Priya: Good to know. For that traffic profile Dedicated or Dedicated + autoscale bursts will be a good fit. We can provision autoscaling in Dedicated pools and recommend batching windows to balance latency/cost.

[07:28] Jon: For Private deployment, how heavy is the ops burden? We're a small infra team.

[07:34] Alex: Private requires more initial setup — networking, KMS, and on-prem packaging if needed. We provide orchestration tooling and runbooks; we also offer managed support add-ons if you want Redwood to operate the control plane. The goal is to make Private as frictionless as possible, but it's still heavier than Hosted.

[07:50] Maya: Any red flags for us?

[07:52] Priya: Only that we should validate multilingual quality — some open models still struggle with Japanese/Korean at long context. We'll run focused tests. Also watch for tokenization blow-up in CJK languages which affects cost.

[08:05] Ellen: Sounds fair. What's the timeline to get benchmarks back?

[08:09] Alex: If you share prompt files by next week (2026-10-07), we can run an initial set and share a results deck by 2026-10-12 and then schedule a deep-dive.

[08:18] Maya: That timeline works. Jon will provision the files and a temp IP whitelist.

[08:23] Jon: Yes I'll share a secure S3 link and whitelist IPs for the test window.

[08:28] Priya: On the model list we'll include quantized variants and a 32k and 64k context run for Llama3 and Falcon. Also Mistral chat 7B as a cost baseline.

[08:38] Maya: A quick question about tool-calling latency — do function calls add a roundtrip overhead? We want them to be deterministic and fast.

[08:45] Priya: Function calls are synchronous from the model's perspective; the overhead depends on your backend. We can pre-validate and stub certain operations during inference to reduce latency; you'll see the breakdown in the benchmark results.

[08:57] Alex: Anything else?

[08:59] Ellen: One last: compliance — can you provide ISO/SOC certificates and a whitepaper on data flows?

[09:05] Alex: Yes we'll attach SOC 2 and data flow diagrams in the follow-up.

[09:09] Maya: Great. That covers it for us. Thanks.

[09:12] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll recap and send next steps.

Recap / Next steps aloud: Alex to send pricing + SOC2 docs; Priya to share benchmark plan and slides; Halcyon to provide prompts and whitelist IPs. Schedule deep-dive the week of 2026-10-12.

End of transcript.
